utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Madam Registrar, could you kindly call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, this is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor v. Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All the accused are here, all the Defence teams are present and everyone is present, yes. And Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye for the Prosecution. The witness is already in his place. Mr. Tanic, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome back. I hope you've had time for a good rest. We are going to resume your testimony and hopefully finish it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, good afternoon, Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Tanic.

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You'll be glad to hear I only have a few questions after reading my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would ask, Mr. President, with the assistance of the usher, that a document be given to the witness. It's a document which was given to my colleague from the Prosecution, and it's simply an extract from his interview with the Prosecution. The number of this document in e-court is 1D267, but I don't think it's required to put it on the e-court or the ELMO, as long as the witness can read the little segment I want to refer him to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic -- can you hear me, Mr. Tanic?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. First of all, I'd like to say that this question refers to something you mentioned yesterday in response to a question from the Prosecution. You said that you saw, in Orahovac, a policeman in uniform who was from Doboj. For the purposes of my colleague, that was on page 24 yesterday, lines 18 to 21. And I would just like to clarify a bit this issue with you, so I would like you to look at the document which was just given to you. On the first page of this document, where it says at the bottom: "15 of 16", and there is a part of this document which is in a box, and I would just like you to read for yourself what is in that box. And this is -- it comes from your interview that you gave to the Office of the Prosecution in June of 2002. I will read the English version for the sake of the Trial Chamber. Question: "When did you learn that the Doboj police was present at Orahovac?" Answer: "As soon as I arrived, there was a big man. There was a big man in police uniform, a blue uniform, who said he was from Doboj, so they were talking. I did not ask him anything or --" and then it stops there for a second question. Do you read this in your language before you now?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd now like to refer you to the third page in the document that you have before you, and this third page bears the number 1 of 155 at the bottom. And again there is a box there which I will read in English, and I would ask you to read it in your own language. And it goes like this: Question: "Okay. Did you meet these men in blue camouflage uniform at Orahovac school?" The response: "On the road in front of the school." Question: "Was he the only one in this -- in such blue uniform or you also noticed some more people in uniforms?" Response: "I don't know. I just spotted him." Question: "Did you speak to him?" Answer: "No, I did not talk to him, but some people around were talking about -- uh-huh. There is a unit from Doboj, and the guy is also from Doboj." Can you read this in your language before you today?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I now refer you to a third segment also in the document that is before you, and this time it begins on the fourth page of the document, at the bottom where it says "2 of 155". For the sake of the interpreters, it's page 87 of the document 1D267. This was just your answer, and it goes as follows: "There was a rumour that a police unit was present, so not military police unit, but regular police unit that was present in the area." Question: "But you did not see any people who were regular police in the area, did you?" You responded by a question: "You mean regular police investigator?" "The MUP." Your answer was: "Except that one guy, I did not." Did you read this in your language before you today?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my question is very simple. I would simply like you to confirm that other than this one man or big man dressed in a blue uniform, the possibility of a unit from the MUP being present was nothing but a rumour; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see anyone except for this one person I told you about. But you can see from this interview that once you mention something, then it goes round in circles. So in various places you have different answers, depending on the approach taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the idea, Mr. Tanic, that there was a unit present is only something that you heard, but it was nothing but a rumour; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I stated, with the exception of that one person I didn't see anyone else. Now, whether he was from there, I don't know myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I move to my next question, and I will ask that the document 3D84 be placed on e-court, please. Mr. Tanic, I will ask you to look in the screen before you- thank you, madam usher, and I have one more question where I need to go back for him to see again. Mr. Tanic, do you recognise the area which is depicted on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There's the school, the yard and the cultural centre and the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I will ask you to mark just three things on this sketch, again with the assistance of the usher. We will be giving you a pen, and I would simply like you to make a circle where the stairs that you mentioned yesterday are located.

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find my way on this sketch. I can't see the main road here. These stairs are somewhere behind the cultural centre, somewhere there. Whether it's closer to one end of the building or the other, I think it was closer to the end of the building closer to the school. I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just draw a circle where you put a little mark in red?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may be wrong, though, because it seems that if I err by one metre, this can cause a big problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I understand your concerns, but your answer is fully in the transcript. Now, my second question on this drawing or on this sketch is whether you can tell the Trial Chamber whether the house where you had coffee with two other persons, if that house is to the left of the stairs indicated in red or to the right, meaning not on this sketch.

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the house on the sketch. It should be somewhere here behind, or rather you can see it from the stairs looking north. The stairs are not facing the road, and from the stairs, which are slanting, you can see the houses, one or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I would just ask you to again take the pen that was given to you, changing colours, any other colour, and simply draw -- make an "X" in the general or approximate area where the house was, the house where you had coffee. Just the general area.

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: What if I make a mistake? Somewhere here. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, yesterday you referred to in your testimony to the house of a Mrs. Vidovic, where you went. Can you confirm that the house of Mrs. Vidovic is not found on this sketch?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can't be seen, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I would like you to look at the sketch, and you see where you have the word "Krizevici Put Orahovac." Do you see these words?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, on that road, I would like you to put, completely to the right of the sketch, an arrow which indicates the direction where you were walking to reach the house of Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know now. You have to get out first. I have to reach the Tuzla-Zvornik road. How can I draw a line? I don't know the roads too well. I would have to go out to the main road. That's what I did. Now, where the main road is, I can't see that. So from this road, I went to the main road and then on foot for about a kilometre. They measured the distance to Mira's house. I'll make a mistake, I can't do it. It may appear that I went in the opposite direction. I don't know what to put.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And all I'm asking of you, Mr. Tanic, is to indicate whether you were walking towards the left of the sketch or towards the right of the sketch to reach Mrs. Vidovic's house.

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I would have to see where the main road is and where this road joins it. I can't draw it, I simply can't. So I went to the main road, and along that main road on foot, the road going from Tuzla to Zvornik. Mira's house is on the main road. Zvornik-Tuzla or Tuzla-Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tanic, the main road, is it on the left of the sketch or on the right of the sketch?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't have a good sense of orientation here. Why is that so important? But if it is important, I really don't know the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tanic, I'm asking you if you stand on that road and you face the Dom Kultur, and you want to go to Mrs. Vidovic's house, do you turn right or do you turn left? That's a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't answer on the basis of this. I really don't know. I don't know Orahovac very well. I know somehow from the by-road you get close to the school, so I went from this road that passes the school to the main road. Now, which side that is, I don't know. I simply don't know anything on the basis of this sketch. All I can say is that I reached the main road, and her house is one kilometre 200 metres. Somebody measured it, I think. That is the distance, about a kilometre and a half from the school to her house. And I can't tell you now which -- where I was standing. You know where the road is. It's still there. I simply can't give you a precise answer. I don't know. I can't orientate myself. I can't show an arrow saying that I went this way or that way. I may make a mistake. So I don't know. So I did go to the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will leave this, Mr. Tanic, and I will simply ask, in the corner of this document, simply to put your initials and today's date, the 24th of April. Thank you, and I don't think -- madam usher, we can save this document as it is, and I would ask the document be introduced in evidence at the end. We can save, and I'll move on to my next question. Mr. Tanic, during your testimony, and I'm not referring you to any statement or interview, or your testimony, but I'm just saying that you made reference to stories that you heard and rumours that you heard. I would simply ask you: Would you agree with me that in that specific period, there were numerous stories and rumours flying around in the area? Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were, yes, probably there were various stories. And I mentioned only one here yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. My next question has to do with Mr. Cedo Jovic. You mentioned, in response to one of my questions yesterday, that he was there on the road with you. Can you confirm that Mr. Jovic --

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: His task there was to protect those who were detained in the gym; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know. We were on the road. Now, what he was doing, I don't know. I think I said earlier on, too, that we were on the road to prevent any other people from going inside, civilians and women.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one last question for you, Mr. Tanic. Again, I will ask you to take the document which was handed to you. I don't know if you still have this document before you, and to switch -- to go to the last page of this document. At the bottom of the page in your language, it says "14 of 155". Do you see the text that is in the box? I would like you to read this text for yourself, and I will read the English version. For the sake of the interpreters, this is page 99 of the document in e-court. What you said then is the following: "I don't want to -- to comment any names of any politicians, but it is a known fact that politicians did not do anything to stop this. I mean, civilian authorities in general. All those civilian authorities were aware of what was going, like I was. You know, they did not stop -- they did not do anything to stop it." Do you stand by this comment today?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tanic. I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. So let's go through the list once more. The Beara team?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Meek. The Borovcanin? Do you confirm that have you no questions? Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we do confirm, Your Honour, we have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Faveau, for Miletic, you stated yesterday that you wouldn't have. Do you confirm?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse or Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just a few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Tanic, you'll be glad to hear your period of giving evidence is almost over. I've just got a few questions for you, and I appear for Vinko Pandurevic who was the commander of the Zvornik Brigade in 1995. Do you understand the phrase "conscientious objector"?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In 1992, when mobilisation took place in Zvornik, you were philosophically opposed to fighting, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, and I still am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And because of that, you asked whether you could serve in the military in a non-combat capacity?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask. I couldn't ask. This was due to circumstances that the events took such a turn, but I see that you're heading towards asking me how I had a rifle. I said in my statement, I pointed out, because somebody from the rear came and said the prisoners are escaping, and that was the only reason. And I believed it, and that's what I did. I didn't go there with a rifle to do I don't know what. I -- that is how I spent the whole war. And conscientious objector is an expression that I'm not familiar with, but I realise now where you're going.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. That wasn't where I was going. I was going to suggest to you that nobody gave you any difficulties in providing you with a non-combat role throughout the three years of the war, did they?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think you may have to repeat your answer, because it hasn't appeared on the transcript and the interpreters haven't picked it up. Did you say nobody did give you any difficulty in providing you with a non-combat role throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the whole war was a difficulty. Nobody had a permanent position throughout the war. There were no guarantees, no rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your role was as a cashier in the financial services of the Zvornik Brigade, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I think you may have already told us, but in case you haven't, you had a small office on the ground floor of the Standard building?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You were not required to stay in the barracks overnight, and you frequently went home on your bicycle, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Indeed, even during the course of the day, you --

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not -- it's not that I asked for permission. I went AWOL. There was a risk involved. I never asked anyone for permission to go home. I just went.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, your direct superior as a cashier was the chief of financial services, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And for most of the war, that was a man named Drago Sakotic?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And financial services was part of the organ for logistics, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that included not just finances, but medical services, the quartermaster's stores and the like?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you about Mijatovic Miladin. He was a man who, at the start of the war, was a battalion commander in Baljkovica, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where exactly he was a battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that he was injured in 1992 and spent much of the war in hospital and convalescing?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And like you, he was assigned at Standard, non-combat duties, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But he was not your superior, was he?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And he had no authority to give you an order on the 14th of July, did he?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I didn't even understand it as an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, that's very helpful. Was Drago Sakotic present at Standard on the 14th of July, when you got in the truck and went to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember. At Standard, I don't think he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: There was another man from whom you sometimes took instructions. His name was Petko Milosevic. Was he there?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. I really don't know. In that period, some changes occurred, a hand-over -- takeover between Drago and Petko, but I don't know exactly at what time. I don't know who was there then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, can I ask you this: Did you verify with any superior officer that it was okay for you to do what Mijatovic Miladin suggested?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. I've already stated that. I wasn't even thinking. He just came, said in passing, "Take your rifle and go." It was not a classic order. I heard people were running away. I took my rifle and went, and the rest of the story you've already heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one last question: Did you ever report to Drago Sakotic what had happened on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Or any other of your superiors?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tanic. I have no more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Mr. Vanderpuye, do you have a re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, we have no re-examination. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Judge Kwon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just apologise to Counsel Stojanovic, because in those notes of mine, I had written something of a personal nature, and there was a second paragraph saying that he asked the same question as the Prosecutor. I'm sorry, I was in two different positions, in two different stages, in the Prosecution stage and the Defence stage. I want to ask, is it appropriate that -- and it's very difficult to be on two chairs. I don't know. I mean -- and what does it mean for the future? If I'm a Prosecution witness, can I also be a Defence witness? That's what I wanted to ask, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm afraid we cannot provide you with an answer to any of your questions, Mr. Tanic. Your testimony ends here, but of course you're free to inquire with the Victims and Witnesses Unit. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we bid you goodbye, Mr. Tanic, may I take you back, please, to the last two questions by Mr. Haynes. The first one was: "Did you ever report to Drago Sakotic what had happened on the 14th of July?" And --

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't even know whether Drago Sakotic was coming to Standard at the time at all. There was a transition of duties between chiefs. Drago Sakotic sometimes came to the brigade to report and then went to the municipality. Whether he was in that same status in that period, I'm not sure. Whether Petko came to replace him after these events, I can't remember now. I don't know whether in that period he was present at Standard, whether he was visiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That confirms your previous answer, which was only of three words: "I don't recall," as it appears on the transcript, was correct. And then Mr. Haynes asked you his very last question: "Or, in other words, did you ever report to any other of your superiors?" What did you answer to that question? If I were to put it again to you: Did you, by any chance, ever report the events of the 14th of July to any of your superiors, what would your answer be?

utterances.speaker: Tanacko Tanic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I did. I talked with the chief of finance about my work, the job I was doing. I didn't report to him about other things. I would just inform him about the state of affairs in the treasury, and I could have related the events to him, perhaps, but it was not a traditional report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that brings your testimony to an end, Mr. Tanic, which also means that you are free to go. Our staff will escort you out of this courtroom and then give you all the assistance you require to facilitate your return back home at the earliest. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, my colleagues, I wish to thank you for having come to give evidence, and I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exhibits, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We have none, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to have admitted in evidence the sketch which was marked by the witness. The original number was 3D94. I would also like to -- sorry, 3D84, 84. And I would also like to have admitted the 3D84 itself. So the blank version as well as the one that was marked. And I guess the number will be 3DIC --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Ninety-four.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- 94. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it there are no other documents to be tendered, so that concludes the evidence of Mr. Tanic. I didn't ask whether you object to the two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the next witness was also a live, a viva voce witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we have an update on how long this witness will take? Mr. Haynes spoke to me briefly, but we do have another witness ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can try to update. I have the Popovic team, 20 minutes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, I had not seen the exhibits. It was the word -- I didn't hear it. Ten minutes, 10 minutes, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Beara team, 45 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Possibly 30, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Nikolic team, one hour and a half?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up to an hour perhaps, Your Honour. It depends on the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the Miletic team, 10 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: We have no questions for this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can I check this is 137, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We have got nothing for 137.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then Pandurevic Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Around 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's where you were, but our rough guess is we will use less of that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Jeremic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, you're required to make a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony you will be testifying and speaking the truth. Please read out that following declaration aloud and that will be your undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer is present in the courtroom and will proceed with his examination-in-chief, after which we will have some cross-examination from the Defence teams. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I would just ask you if you would to keep your voice up, if you could, and maybe move just a little bit closer to the microphone so we don't miss anything you have to say. Okay? Would you please state and spell your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Nebojsa, N-e-b-o-j-s-a. Jeremic, my last name, J-e-r-e-m-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where were you born and raised, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I was born in Zvornik, and I grew up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you are a lawyer by training; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what has your peace-time profession been?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I worked at the tax administration in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just approximately how long have you worked in that capacity, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: You mean before the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Before the war and after the war. Just in total, approximately how long have you worked in that job?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Twenty-one years.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, I want to review with you very briefly your military service history, and if you would just, when I'm done, correct me if I've -- if I've misstated anything, please. You were mobilised in May of 1992, and you served as an infantryman. Then you were assigned to register refugees in the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: After that, you served as an infantryman again in December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at some point in the spring of 1993, you transferred to a particular unit of the Zvornik Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, please, the name of your specialised unit or your particular unit?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I was transferred to the service for combatting crime with the Zvornik Brigade, and that belonged to the military police company.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And just briefly, can you describe how your transfer to that unit came about?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: A friend of mine, Goran Bogdanovic, had already transferred to that unit before me, and since they needed another soldier, he suggested that I transfer too.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell the Trial Chamber who the commander of the military police company was?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Miomir Jasikovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to whom did Mr. Jasikovac report?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: The chief of the security, Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where was your unit based, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: At the barracks, Standard, in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you have your own office there, sir, your unit, that is?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. My service had its own office.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what floor of the Standard barracks was that located on? Just the floor.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'd like you to take a few moments, please, and just describe the function of your crime prevention unit for the Trial Chamber. First of all, just what kinds of crimes did your unit deal with, for example?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: My service dealt with criminal acts within the Zvornik Brigade. In other words, our duty was -- in fact, we were responsible for the fighting men of the Zvornik Brigade, any criminal acts that they may have committed fell within our purview for purposes of investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would this involve crimes of all levels of seriousness or only of a particular level of seriousness, sir? And if it's easier just to describe some examples of types of crimes you dealt with, then feel free to do so as well.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Well, we dealt with all criminal acts committed by members of the Zvornik Brigade, and I mean mobilised fighting men. That included murders; desertion; infliction of wounds; self-infliction of wounds; or self-injury; thefts; absence without official leave; similar things.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And when you describe murders, sir, are you referring to murders that occurred between a Zvornik member and another Zvornik member, Zvornik Brigade member?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just generally speaking in 1995, how busy would you say your unit was?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Well, the service was always busy in the past years before 1995 and in 1995, and the reason, in my opinion, is that it was a large brigade and there was always work for us. Criminal acts were committed all the time, or misdemeanors, so that we were very busy.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You just referred to "us." Other than yourself and Mr. Bogdanovic, who else was in your unit?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: When I said "we," I meant the crime prevention service. That included me, Goran Bogdanovic and Cedo Jovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what types of tasks would you personally perform in connection with your duties, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Most of the time, we were taking statements from soldiers. I'm speaking of the soldiers of the Zvornik Brigade. We wrote orders in the name of battalion commanders. Most often that concerned failure to show up at the front line. We wrote orders in the name of the brigade commander, but also criminal reports. We gathered all the necessary documentation that must accompany criminal reports, such as statements by perpetrators, statements by witnesses, and if the criminal act concerned was more serious, such as a murder, then we worked in cooperation with the civilian police, that is, with the scene-of-crime officers who would photograph and sketch the crime scene while we took statements from witnesses and the perpetrator. We would take a description of the body from the hospital and we would seize the rifle because it was a rifle that was most often used as a weapon, and we sent all the documentation to the military prosecution's office, together with a criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And, sir, in cases where charges would be brought, who actually drafted those charges?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I would draft them, as did Goran Bogdanovic and Cedo Jovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, you refer to orders that you would draft under the signature of the brigade commander. Could you just give the Trial Chamber a couple of examples of the types of orders that you would draft, or your colleagues would draft?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: We would write orders by the brigade commander relating to certain more serious offences committed by members of the brigade. We wrote when the punishment was up to 60 days in prison because, to the best our knowledge, the brigade commander had the right to punish a soldier with a prison term up to 60 days, military prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, just to be clear, to your knowledge and understanding did the brigade commander have that authority independent of any decision by the military prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to make sure. When you say you weren't aware of that, are you saying you don't know whether the brigade commander had that authority or are you saying something else? And I can rephrase the question slightly. Maybe that will help. In your experience, would the brigade need to await approval from the military prosecutor's office before issuing charges or a sentencing order like the one you described, sentencing someone to 60 days in military imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the brigade did not have to wait for approval from the military courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, who signed off on the criminal charges which you and your colleagues wrote up?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: The chief of security, Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you or your two colleagues have the authority on your own to initiate an investigation or draw up charges against a soldier?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't. As far as I know, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And so who would direct you to do so, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: The chief of security, Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during the course of carrying out your various tasks, sir, would you keep Drago Nikolic informed of your progress?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, we would inform him. He was the chief, and we had to keep him informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, on a day-to-day basis, can you describe how you and your colleagues would receive your orders?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Every morning, we would inform the chief of security of the situation in the military detention, and then he would go, I think, to talk to the brigade commander, where the reporting was taking place. And after that, we would go to his office or he would call us up by phone and hand down instructions as to what we should do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, what was your understanding and experience in the brigade as to any daily meetings that Drago Nikolic may have had with the brigade commander, Mr. Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I said that I never attended those meetings, so I don't know how these agreements and discussions took place and what they discussed. I just know that after this reporting, the chief would give us instructions as to what to do, that is, a briefing, actually, after the briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you mentioned that on some occasions you would go to Drago Nikolic's office to receive your orders. On any occasion, would you see Mr. Jasikovac there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And on those occasions in the morning, what was Mr. Jasikovac doing in Mr. Nikolic's office?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: He was -- would also come to receive instructions for his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in Drago Nikolic's absence, who gave you and your colleagues orders?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: His deputy, Milorad Trbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want to focus your attention in a different area for the next few questions. I want to turn your attention to the time immediately following the fall of the Srebrenica enclave. No doubt you recall that period of time. Can you tell the Trial Chamber where you were spending your days and nights during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I spent my days and nights in the barracks in Standard. There was an alert situation, and we were all down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall, sir, at some point after the fall of Srebrenica, seeing some buses while you were at the Standard base?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see -- see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry to interrupt you, but I noted the witness mentioned Mr. Trbic as his -- deputy to Mr. Nikolic. Can I ask the witness what Mr. Trbic's rank was at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, did you understand His Honour's question?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I did understand the question. He was an officer, but I don't know what his rank was. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Back to the buses, sir. Can you please describe for the Trial Chamber what you saw when you saw these buses?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I saw buses passing by the barracks, that Muslim prisoners were in them, and I saw our guards standing in the buses. I don't know whether they were guards of the Zvornik Brigade. In fact, I think they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you able to observe the position of any of these prisoners, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I did observe it. They had their heads bowed and they held their hands above their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say they were above their heads, sir, what do you mean? How were their hands?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: What I meant, like this, behind their necks. [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Indicating that their fingers were interlocked behind their -- behind their heads?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you recall what direction the buses were coming from and what direction they were headed towards as you sit here today, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I do recall. They were coming from the direction of Zvornik or rather further away from Bratunac and they were moving --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes? THE REPORTER: I'm sorry but my computer has just crashed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, all right. Sorry. I saw that there was some disturbance but I saw Mr. Ostojic looking this way and I tried to follow you, Mr. Ostojic. So you have misdirected the Trial Chamber. Yeah, I think we need to wait until this is sorted out. As soon as it is okay please, let us know. Unless you all agree to have the break now rather than in 15 minutes' time. We could do that as well. Okay. Let's have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is everything okay now? THE REPORTER: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much, and thank you for alerting us in a timely fashion. So we go back to your last recorded question, please, line 19 on page 26. And then the witness will start his answer again or repeat his answer which never made it to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to make sure we're on the same page literally, that is the question regarding indicating their fingers interlocked behind their heads or we're down to where I see the direction of the buses question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. That's at line 23 from my transcript. I'll ask the same question and we'll start from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It doesn't tell me what my line -- mine is line 19: "Can you recall what direction the buses were coming from and what direction they were headed to as you sit here today, sir?" And you had started giving your answer when we had a minor calamity.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, if you would just describe for the Court, if you can recall, which direction the buses were coming from and in which direction they were headed.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall. The buses were coming from the direction of Zvornik or further away from Bratunac, and they were moving towards Bijeljina because the Zvornik-Bijeljina road passes by the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where were you, sir, when you saw these buses?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I was in the barracks compound, the Standard barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you see these buses from more than one location at the Standard barracks?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I saw them from within the compound. I can't tell you exactly where I was standing. I was in the compound, and I saw those buses passing by.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. At some time after this day when you saw those buses, did you begin to hear rumours at the brigade? And if so, can you tell the Trial Chamber what those rumours were that you heard?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: After that, I don't know exactly how many days later, I can't give you a date as to when, but I heard that there were executions of Muslims in Orahovac and Pilica. Those were the rumours that were going round in the brigade or, rather, at Standard I heard this from the soldiers. No one said anything officially, but many of them were talking about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I'm not asking you for any particular dates or times, sir, but during these days following the fall of Srebrenica, did you see Drago Nikolic in and around the Standard barracks?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see him in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how about Mr. Trbic, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And Mr. Jasikovac?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you have any specific knowledge as to where they were going on those occasions when you saw them in and out of the barracks?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I had no knowledge as to where they were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to turn your attention to a different topic. I want to ask you some questions about some charges which were brought against a father and son in which your unit had some involvement. Can you tell the Trial Chamber how you first became aware of any allegations against this father and son?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. How did you first come to -- I see you nodding your head. Can you answer the question, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can, I think I can answer the question. At a certain point in time, two Serb combatants were brought to the office. I think it was Djokic Nesko and his son, I don't know his name, and then Drago Nikolic came, the chief in the brigade, and he said that these were our fighters who had assisted the enemy and that criminal charges should be filed against them and an order should be drafted for the brigade commander for military imprisonment of 60 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, were you present, sir, when Drago Nikolic made this statement?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was he, in fact, addressing you, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I think he was addressing me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You indicated that one of your typical duties was to interview witnesses and take statements. Did you actually meet the father and son?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Who did you meet first, sir, and where?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: In the office in which I worked, I met the younger Djokic, that is, the son.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you describe what happened in that meeting, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I remember that the Djokic Jr., that is, the son, he wouldn't admit why he had been brought in, and then the chief, Drago Nikolic, slapped him once, and he told the whole story.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And after he was slapped, what did he say happened, sir, that is, the Jokic son.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: He said that he and his father, Nesko, had tried to help four Muslim men to cross our lines and reach the other side, and they wanted to help them to do this; that they gave them food and clothing, and that their intention was to bring them to our positions and then for them to cross the lines on their own. I'm talking about the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, was the father then brought in to your office?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall whether Drago Nikolic was still in your office when the father was brought in?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes. As the father was in front of the office, which is nearby, he wasn't at any distance, he was standing in front of the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, did you complete the answer to your question? I'm sorry, I couldn't tell whether you were done or not.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So the father was brought in to your office. Did Drago Nikolic, to the best of your recollection, stay in your office for the meeting with the father?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I think he didn't stay long in the office after the son had made his admissions. He left. I don't think he stayed in the office for long.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall whether the son said anything to the father?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he said, "Daddy, I have admitted everything. They know everything. Why don't you tell them, too, what happened?"

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were statements eventually taken from the father and son, sir? And if so, do you recall who took them?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, statements were taken from Nesko Djokic and his son concerning the circumstances that I have described a moment ago, and they were taken by my colleague, Goran Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall the name of the village this father and son were from and where these events took place?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's a place near Zvornik called Lokanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may have 65 ter number 393 displayed on e-court, and I'll be referring to page 1 of the English translation and page 1 of the original B/C/S document for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see a document in front of you on your computer screen?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recognise what that document is?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What is it, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: That's the statement of Nesko Djokic concerning what I just explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could have page 2 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S document shown, please. Perfect, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have an image on your screen?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see the signature at the bottom right of the document?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: My colleague's, Goran Bogdanovic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In the penalty of the fact that his name is typewritten there, do you recognise that handwriting as that of your colleague, Goran Bogdanovic?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now -- and we're done with this document for the time being. Thank you. Did you also interview the Muslim prisoners, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think you mentioned that there were four altogether. How many did you personally interview?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Three, I took the statements of three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you remember who interviewed the fourth?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: My colleague, Cedo Jovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please describe for the Trial Chamber the appearance --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll move on and ask the question again, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not receiving interpretation in English. Yes, but I have had the privilege what I stated in English translated into Serbo-Croat again. Are you receiving interpretation in English? No. So we have this problem which needs to be solved.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Are you on the English channel now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We have always been on the English channel. So I think we can proceed. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we're just having some technical difficulties with the translation channeling. Would you please describe how these four Muslim prisoners appeared when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: First of all, they looked frightened. They were thin. Their clothes were in shreds. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may have 65 ter number 392 displayed on e-court, please, page 1 of the English and the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see that document in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: That's the statement that we took from those Muslim prisoners. This is the statement of Almir Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you can take a look at the first line just above where it says "Statement," just for the record, can you indicate the village and opstina that's indicated for this witness?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Shall I say the name?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you would, please, sir, just read it.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Almir Halilovic, son of Suljo and Dika, born on the 25th of August, 1980, in Bajramovici village, Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If we could have page 3 of the B/C/S shown and page 2 of the English, and if we could go to the bottom. Thank you. Sir, do you see this document, this new page in front of you?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is that your signature on the lower right corner there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: It's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may have 65 ter 389 displayed as well. Do you recognise what this is, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is it, please?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: It's a statement by a Muslim prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you just read into the record the name of the prisoner and his biographical information that's indicated in that first sentence? Just read that in briefly, if you would.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Sakib Kiviric, son of Salko and mother, Hadzira, born on the 24th of June, 1964, in Jagodnja, Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could have page 3 of the B/C/S and page 2 of the English displayed, please. And again, sir, just turn your attention to the lower right-hand corner. Is that your signature there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 390, please? Looking at the first page of the document, is this also a statement of one of the Muslim prisoners that you took, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, would you just briefly read the biographical information into the record?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Emin Mustafic, son of Rifet and mother Rukija, born on the 7th of October 1969, in Drinjaca, Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could see page 3 of the B/C/S, please, and page 2 of the English. Again, sir, do you recognise your signature in the lower right-hand corner of this statement?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Lastly, sir, I want to show you 65 ter 391. Do you recognise this as the statement of the fourth Muslim prisoner?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you would just read the -- that biographical information, please.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Fuad Djozic, born to father Senusija and mother Rukija, on the 2nd of May, 1965, in Zegojno, Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we may have the third page of the B/C/S and the second page of the English, please. Do you see who has signed the page at the bottom right-hand corner here, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I see the signature and who it belongs to.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And as you sit here, can you tell the Trial Chamber whether or not you were familiar with that individual's handwriting, and if you would please just state the name of the person whose signature is there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: You can -- the statement was taken by Cedo Jovic, and he signed. I cannot say with absolute certainty that it's his signature, but I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, was there any sort of identification procedure undertaken during your investigation concerning these four prisoners who were aided by the father and son?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 394 displayed on e-court, please? Sir, what is this document before you on your computer?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: It's a record that was made concerning the identification made of father and son, Djokic, by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it indicates that there were three persons present. Who does it indicate were present during identification?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Second Lieutenant Drago Nikolic, chief of security; Goran Bogdanovic, chief of service for the crime prevention; and another member of the crime prevention service, Goran Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. You just -- I'm looking at your answer here, and you've indicated that Drago Nikolic, chief of security, was present, Goran Bogdanovic, chief of security for the -- chief of service for the crime prevention, and another member of the crime prevention service who you again identified as Goran Bogdanovic. Would you just please take a look at the document again and I ask you whether that's accurate or whether --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's mistake, it's Nebojsa Jeremic, the third name.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Don't worry about the question. Don't worry about answering the question, you've answered it already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, interpreter, and thank you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we see page 3 of the document in B/C/S, which is page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see in the lower right corner the signature, and can you tell us who that is?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I see it. It's Goran Bogdanovic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And there appears also to be a stamp on top of that signature. Do you recognise that stamp, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I recognise the stamp of our brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I apologise for this. If we could go back to page 1 of each document in B/C/S and English. I just wanted to ask you one question about one line.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I would direct your attention to the portion of the document that starts immediately after the number "3" where your name is listed. If you could just read that first line, please.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: "Following operative information that there is reason to believe that Djokic Nesko and his son, Slobodan, extended assistance to the enemy." Their identification, followed by four enemy soldiers who had been arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And, sir, I just asked that question because I think the English translation, for those of us who are following along, may be incorrect as translated, and I just wanted to verify what was in the B/C/S original for the record. May we have 65 ter 385 on e-court, please. Do you see the document in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court what, if anything, this document orders? [Realtime transcript did not include answer symbol]

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: This is a decision for detention in the duration of three days for Nesko Djokic and his son, Slobodan.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we may turn to page 3 of the B/C/S and page 2 of the English, please. Do you recognise the handwriting on the signature there, sir, in the lower right-hand corner? Sorry, you need to speak audibly into the record. I see you're nodding your head. Are you receiving interpretation, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I hear perfectly well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recognise the handwriting at the signature?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And whose handwriting is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: It's the signature of the chief of security, Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, do you see a stamp -- do you recognise that stamp that's there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I recognise the stamp and the military PO box.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you had some comments about this document for me. Would you care to share them with the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: What I said was that this order for military detention was not written by me in this way and that I cannot identify this because we used a different format and a different style in writing within our service in relation to orders for detention in the duration of three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, based on your recollection of these events and your participation in this investigation, is the document factually correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, the disposition seems to be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you have any reason to doubt its authenticity, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I do not doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The last document I want to show you, sir, is 65 ter number 386.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, no objection, but page 12, line 9, I think the Prosecutor asked a question and then there was an answer, but the answer follows right with the question, so just for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, since previously I noticed that the lines and page do not -- at least what I have do not correspond with Mr. Thayer's, could you read out to me, please, the question, yes, so that I point out immediately --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, on my screen the question was: "And can you tell the Court what, if anything, this document orders?" And then following that is: "This is a decision for detention in the duration of three days for Nesko Djokic and his son, Slobodan." I believe that was the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. So we're talking of lines 8 to 10 on page 12, at least on what we have here, and these need to be separated, line 8 and the first word on line 9 stay where they are, and the rest from "this is a decision" right up to "his son, Slobodan," the next line, will be marked as being the answer given by the witness to the previous question. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I thank my learned colleague for that intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again, sir, we're just having some technical difficulties, nothing for you to be concerned about. Do you see the document in front of you, a new document on your screen, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is this, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: It's a criminal report to the military prosecutor's office in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may have page 3 of the B/C/S and page 2 of the English. Again, do you recognise the handwriting of the signature here, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And whose is it, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: It is the signature of the chief of security, Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, there's a stamp for the brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this is a report concerning the charges against the father and son, is that correct, just to be clear?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, as you sit here today, do you know for certain whether or not your unit actually wrote up charges against the father and son?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I do not remember. I did not write a criminal report, if that's what you are referring to, and I don't recollect whether an order was written by the brigade commander, signing 60 days of military imprisonment which I was told should be written.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, were you transferred to other duties in and around this time or shortly thereafter?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: On the 26th of July, I went to do work duty lasting three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, just a few more questions for you, sir. During this investigation, where were the four Muslims held?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I think they were in the military detention room, which was inside the barracks, the Standard barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And on -- just what floor, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: It was on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you have any idea where the father and son were held?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And with respect to those four Muslim prisoners, sir, when was the last time you recall seeing them?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I saw them for the last time in the office when they were making their statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea how long they were kept at Standard?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you have any information concerning what happened to them ultimately?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned that at some point many people in the brigade were talking about executions that had taken place at Orahovac and Pilica. To your knowledge, did anyone in the brigade request the military prosecutor's office to conduct an investigation into those executions that were reported and rumoured?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, to your knowledge were you or anyone in your unit, that is, your crime prevention unit, ever instructed to conduct an investigation into the executions at Orahovac and Pilica?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if an investigation were to be ordered into such events, who would have ordered you to do so, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Drago Nikolic, the chief of security of the brigade. That is my opinion, because he was the one who issued orders to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I thank you. I have no further questions for you at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thayer, as I stated earlier, I have got several different teams who have expressed their intention to cross-examine the witness. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will not cross-examine this witness, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. How are you?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Thank you, I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: A few questions is all I have, and first off: You gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on 12th of January, 2006, which you reviewed and confirmed on the 22nd day of April, 2007, with only two changes; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you are referring to. Which two changes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, the first correction you said you had, or change or correction, would be that you did not write report, rather you would write, among other things, sentencing orders and criminal charges. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. I'm saying that again. I didn't write reports. I wrote orders and criminal charges, but not reports to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And the only other correction that you made from your 12 January 2006 statement to the Office of the Prosecutor was you drew a new sketch; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, it is true, sir, that you would have had to have reviewed thoroughly your 12 January 2006 statement in order to tell Mr. Thayer of the two changes; isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I read the statement. I read the statement three days ago, I think it was when I read the statement, but I don't really understand what you are asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: My only question was: You thoroughly reviewed that statement, now you say, three days ago? That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not sure there's a question on the record, and that may be what's going on, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall I intervene?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The witness answered, "yes," I'm sorry. The witness answered, "yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "Yes, I read the statement," he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to ask you a couple of questions about that statement. First, every morning the commander of the military police, the military company, the police company, the Zvornik Brigade, would give you orders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: It is not correct. Orders were given to me by Drago Nikolic, the chief of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And that was after a daily morning briefing; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
utterances.text: If you're meaning briefing -- if you mean briefing, I never attended those briefings with the brigade commander, but I know that they took place every morning, and after that in the service we would receive instructions from Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, correct, and I didn't mean to insinuate that you personally attended those meetings. Let's go a little further. You did indicate in your statement that from time to time the military police company commander might give you some orders, but you also received orders from Drago Nikolic and his deputy, Trbic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it would be perhaps useful if the witness could see the entire portion of the statement to which my learned colleague is referring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you agree to that, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I don't disagree, Judge. 3D107 is the English, and I don't have the number for the B/C/S, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If someone could assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So if we could put just paragraph 5, the first page, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: First off --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, it's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I think we'll have to switch back to the page before where paragraph 5 starts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, could you just read paragraph 5 to yourself, and when you're finished with the two lines on this page, we'll have it switched to the next page.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA JEREMIC
